job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Grace Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Grace. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I keep a spreadsheet for everything, so I can tell you my day by the hour. Mornings are lectures for my master's in software engineering at Marlow University, afternoons are study and applications, and four nights a week I work the late desk in the library, 10pm to 2am, for about 600 a month. I live in student housing with three flatmates, and I cook in batches on Sundays to save money. Most days I'm in bed by three.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about your first degree.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Software engineering, a pass. My final project was a bus timetable app for a rural council, and the council actually used it for a few months, which I'm proud of. But my exam marks were average, and I had no internship because I was working nights even then. My dad runs a small dairy farm two hours away and it barely breaks even, so no help from him. I owe about twenty-nine thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool but not a revolution, and that people shouldn't plan their lives around hype. I'd say the same at the library desk: it saves me some time on boilerplate code and not much else. If I'm honest, I'd probably say it with a shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still worried because the problem is the same as today. Entry-level software jobs are thin near here, my grade is average, and I have almost no savings. The jobs I see ask for two years of experience and a portfolio that I only half have. It doesn't feel like AI's fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep the library shifts, and make the timetable app a proper portfolio piece with a write-up. I'd apply to ten jobs a week and add three small open-source fixes to my GitHub. I use AI tools now and then, mostly to explain error messages, and I'd keep that up. I'd also ask the council if they'd give me a reference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady but tired. I'm managing, and I know I'm one bad month from not managing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a bad month look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like the laptop breaking. I've got maybe 300 saved, and a new laptop is more than that. I'd have to borrow from a flatmate, or ask my dad, who'd say yes and then skip a feed bill. I try not to think about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are you doing about the experience problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Open-source fixes, small ones, because a project maintainer is the closest thing to a manager I can get for free. Last month I fixed a date bug in a calendar library, and the maintainer replied with a thank-you. That one comment is worth more to me than my last exam.

say: I'd say it's a useful tool but not a **revolution**, and people shouldn't plan their lives around hype.
I'd say it with a shrug.
think: My problem is the same as today: **thin local jobs**, an average grade and almost no savings.
Most job posts ask for two years of experience I only half have.
do: Keep the late **library shifts** and finish the master's.
Turn the timetable app into a **portfolio piece** and ask the council for a reference.
Apply to ten jobs a week and add small **open-source fixes**.
feel: **Steady but tired**; I'm one bad month from not managing.
S0.quote: A project maintainer is the closest thing to a manager I can get for free.
fieldNote: Methodical and **spreadsheet-driven**: tracks hours, savings and applications.

Uses AI tools occasionally, consistent with steady adaptability.

steps.text: Keep the late library desk shifts four nights a week
Apply to ten jobs a week with the timetable app as the lead project
Add three small open-source fixes to my GitHub

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the first time I've felt the ground move, because the stuff it takes over is the stuff a junior developer does: boilerplate, tests, bug fixes. I'd say it plainly to my flatmates and mean it. I wouldn't panic online, but I'd talk about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think fewer graduate posts get advertised and more of them go to people with better marks and internships. I'd be one of the people squeezed out, because my pass grade and no internship are the first things a filter drops. My steady side says people still need someone to check the output, and that might be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim at roles where a person checks and runs software: testing, support engineering, and anything in the public sector. I'd take any paid junior post, even a poorly paid one. I'd build more with AI help and show the council what I did, because I trust things once I've seen them work. And I'd ask my course tutor for a letter that explains my mark and the project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, then more anxious the more I think about it. I'm an organised person, and I'd hate to feel the plan wobbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you trust things once you've seen them work. What would convince you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I see my classmates getting hired with their AI skills, then I'll go all in. Until then I'd use it for one project and see what happens. That's how I've done everything, and it's usually saved me from wasting time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad. The dairy farm has software for milking now, and a lot of the paperwork gets done by an app. If that gets better, then he'd need me home to do it, or he'd do it badly. I'd worry about the farm more than about me.

I'd say it plainly to my flatmates.
think: Fewer graduate posts get advertised, and my **pass grade** and no internship are the first things a filter drops.

feel: **Uneasy** first, then more anxious; I hate feeling the plan wobble.

fieldNote: Software engineering is the most **exposed** field in this cohort, and she knows it.

Worries as much about her father's farm paperwork as about herself.

steps.text: Apply for testing, support engineering and public sector roles
Build a second small project with AI help and write it up
Ask my tutor for a reference letter that explains my mark

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast for anyone to be ready, and that governments should act now with retraining and income support. I'd say it to my dad, to my tutor and to the council. But I know that would sound dramatic, and I'd feel odd saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm quite afraid. Software is my field, and I think it's the first field to go. I'd finish the master's right when it arrives, with a pass grade and a debt of twenty-nine thousand. I don't have a plan B, because I put everything into this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for work that isn't only a screen: anything near the farm, in logistics, in the council, in energy. I'd go home on weekends and help my dad with the milking, which I haven't done since I was 17. I'd also ask the university what support is available for graduates, and I'd stop buying anything I don't need. And I'd try to learn the AI tools in earnest, because I'd feel stupid not to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cold and shaky, and a bit guilty. I chose this degree because I thought it was safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you put everything into this one. What would a plan B look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the farm. Dad's herd is small, but he needs help with the records, the milk contracts and the machines. It wouldn't pay me, but it would feed me. I'd hate to go backwards, but I'd hate to go hungry more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the AI tools sooner and more seriously. I used them for error messages, but I never let them do a whole task, and now I'd wish I had. I'd also have taken that unpaid internship in second year, when the council offered it.

say: I'd say two years is **too fast** and governments should act now with retraining and income support.
I'd say it to my dad, my tutor and the council.
think: Software is the **first field** to go, and I'd finish the master's just as it arrives.
I have no plan B, because I put everything into this one.
do: Look for work that isn't only a screen: **logistics**, council or energy.
Go home on weekends to help my dad with **milking** and the farm records.
Ask the university what **support** exists for graduates.
feel: **Cold and shaky**, and a bit guilty; I chose this degree because I thought it was safe.
S2.quote: I chose this degree because I thought it was safe.
fieldNote: Her field is the one most directly **hit**, and her emotional reaction shows it.

steps.text: Apply for logistics, council and energy roles that mix screen and site work
Go home on weekends to help my dad with milking and records
Stop all spending that isn't rent, food or travel to lectures
Use AI tools on a whole project to learn them properly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to prepare if you start now. I'd say we should move training toward working with AI and put money behind it, and I'd say employers should still take graduates. I'd say it calmly, because panic doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious, not alarmed. If I get a first job within a year or so, I'd have maybe three years of experience before the field changes a lot. That could be enough to move into a role like AI operations or something near the farm. If I don't get the first job, I'm in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take any junior software job, and put 150 a month into savings. I'd get serious with the AI tools and learn how to supervise them, because checking output is a skill. I'd also see if I could use my timetable app experience for another rural council, since small councils can't afford big firms. And I'd keep the library desk job until a proper salary arrived.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More settled than the first two. I'd still check the spreadsheet every day, but I'd feel I can steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said small councils can't afford big firms. How would you reach them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The council that used my app has a regional network. I'd ask the clerk to introduce me, then offer a free pilot for one route and charge only if it worked. It's a small plan, but small plans are the ones I can actually carry out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the spreadsheet say about your first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Income 600 from the library, maybe 1,800 from a junior job, minus rent and food, and about 150 a month into savings. If I'm lucky, in twelve months I'd have a cushion of a thousand. It's boring, but a thousand would be the first one I've ever had.

I'd say it calmly, because panic doesn't help.

Without that first job, I'm in trouble.

Offer a free **pilot** of the timetable app to another rural council.

S3.quote: Small plans are the ones I can actually carry out.
fieldNote: She turns anxiety into **numbers**: income, savings and a target cushion of a thousand.

steps.text: Take any junior software job offered within a year
Put 150 a month into a savings account
Learn to supervise AI tools on a real project
Offer a free pilot of the timetable app to another rural council

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The scenario is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a different conversation. I'd say it's a chance to adjust the education system, and I'd say I'd be fine if I started sensible habits now. I'd say it to my flatmates over Sunday dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be uneasy rather than anxious. I'd have a decade to pay off debt, build a career and maybe own a small flat. The thing I'd watch is whether my skills stay useful, because software moves fast. But I think I could adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, take a software job, and spend the first three years paying down debt and saving. Then I'd decide whether to move to AI supervision, or to something like public sector systems where there'll still be a need for human sign-off. I'd also help my dad modernise the farm's records. I'd learn something new every year, even if it's just a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Not thrilled, but okay. It's the first time I feel the spreadsheet could end up with a surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a surplus mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can say yes to something without checking the balance. A trip home without counting the train fare. A new laptop before the old one dies. It sounds small, and for me it's a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get complacent. A decade is long enough to relax and then wake up with a skill nobody wants. I'd put a yearly review in my calendar, like a service on a car.

Choose between AI supervision and public-sector systems after three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because software is my field and I'd have no time to move. What would help is a graduate scheme that actually exists, some protection for people with student debt, and honest advice about where to aim. A mentor in the public sector would help too, someone who'd tell me which jobs will last.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not asking for pity. I'm organised, I work, and I'd do the job well if somebody gave me a start. What frightens me is the gap between graduating and anyone noticing.

headlineQuote: What frightens me is the gap between graduating and anyone noticing.
portrait: Grace is 24, doing a master's in **software engineering**, and works four late nights a week at the library desk.
She has a pass, **no internship** and about twenty-nine thousand of debt, and her father's dairy farm can't help.
She plans everything in a **spreadsheet** and trusts new things once she has seen them work.
Her own field is the **most exposed** to thinking AI, so she's alarmed in the fast scenarios.
She falls back on small, doable plans: a free pilot for a rural council, savings and her father's **farm**.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because software is her field and there'd be no time to move.
whatWouldHelp: A real **graduate scheme**, protection for people with student debt and honest advice about where to aim.
A **public-sector mentor** who knows which jobs will last.
